feed.title: Re: Safer sighashes and more granular SIGHASH_NOINPUT

entry.title: Re: Safer sighashes and more granular SIGHASH_NOINPUT
entry.summary:
Replacing traditional OP_IF ... OP_ENDIF sequences in Bitcoin scripts with a Merklized Script tree structure enables more efficient and private conditional execution. This approach organizes possible script branches into a binary Merkle tree, where only the executed path needs to be revealed, preserving privacy for unused branches. However, constructing a Merkle root for such a tree involves hashing all combinations of script branches, which leads to significant computational demands as the tree depth increases.
The computation time required to build a complete Merkle root grows exponentially with the depth of the tree. For each additional level, the number of leaf nodes—and thus the number of hash operations—doubles. As a result, for trees with considerable depth, such as those ranging from 20 to 30, performance on typical consumer hardware may degrade to impractical levels. The feasibility of this approach depends heavily on the efficiency of the hashing implementation and the hardware used.
There is an expressed need for benchmarks or empirical estimates regarding the time required to compute Merkle roots at various depths, particularly for full binary trees on standard consumer-grade machines. Understanding these performance characteristics is essential before adopting Merklized Script trees with high complexity in real-world scenarios.
